title: Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald Applicant against Finlay George Morrison Respondent [2026] SLC 3
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2026] SLC 3,
Case reference: SLC/16/24

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr T Campbell

Donald Norman MacLennan MacDonald
Applicant
against
Finlay George Morrison
Respondent

Crofting Register: Challenge to first registration

Croft 1 Ardvourlie

Applicant: Kermack, Lay Representative

Respondent: Rudd, Solicitor; Murchison Law

13 February 2026

Introduction

[1] Ardvourlie is a crofting township on the Isle of Harris, comprising two crofts and a common grazing. The applicant is the tenant of Croft 2, which does not appear on the Crofting Register. The respondent is the tenant of the neighbouring Croft 1 which is registered in the Crofting Register under number C770. Croft 1 was first registered in December 2014 on the application of the landlord, the North Harris Trust.

[2] The applicant seeks an order under section 14(4) of the Crofting Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 modifying the entry in the Crofting Register, contending that Croft 1 was registered with substantially enhanced boundaries so that it wrongly includes an area of land at the route of the former public road lying between the two crofts and the new A859 public road (land for which was resumed in 2004).

[3] By interlocutor dated 23 May 2024, the Court exercised its discretion in terms of section 12(5) of the 2010 Act, on cause shown, to allow this application to be dealt with as if it had been made before the end of the statutory 9 month period in respect that the applicant’s failure to make this application timeously - and lack of knowledge until 2023 of the fact of first registration of Croft 1 - was excusable in respect that he did not receive notification, either of the application for registration or of the registration itself.

[4] Other than in respect of one small area of ground, the respondent opposes the application.

[5] A diet of proof was held at Stornoway Sheriff Court in October 2025. The Court also took evidence of some witnesses at Ardvourlie and carried out a sight inspection. The applicant was represented by Mr Kermack, a retired solicitor acting on this occasion as a duly authorised lay representative. Mr Rudd, solicitor appeared for the respondent. Following the proof diet parties lodged supplementary written submissions.

[6] The plan which accompanied the 2014 application by the landlord for first registration of Croft 1 divides Croft 1 into three areas and shows the route of the new public road which was constructed in the period 2004 ‑ 2007 and runs between Areas 1 and 2 (on the east side of the road) and Area 3 (on the west side of the road). Area 3 denotes the apportionment to Croft 1 from the common grazings and is not controversial for present purposes. A detail of that plan appears below:

Figure 1 – Detail from plan from 2014 application for first registration of Croft 1

[7] A further plan was lodged by the applicant as his production 20 which is helpful in illustrating the areas in dispute. A detail of that plan is reproduced at Figure 2 below.

Figure 2 – Detail from applicant’s production 20

[8] Mr Kermack explained (and it was not disputed) that the areas outlined in red in Figure 2 are a projection of the boundaries contained on Figure 1, superimposed on the 1973 Ordnance Survey map for Ardvourlie, which map dates from some three decades before construction of the new road. Three areas are shaded blue on the Figure 2, two within the northern-most section outlined in red (which corresponds with Area 1 on Figure 1) and one in the southern-most section outlined in red (which corresponds with Area 2 on Figure 1). The applicant contends that the three areas shaded blue were wrongly included with the registered extent of Croft 1. The smallest of the blue shaded areas is within the northern-most section and is Kosiden house and garden (“Kosiden”). Parties agree that Kosiden was wrongly included within the registered extent of Croft 1, having previously been resumed from crofting in 1963, and accordingly should be removed from the Crofting Register. The dispute between parties relates to the two remaining areas shaded blue, referred to hereinafter respectively as the NDA (the Northernmost Disputed Area) and the SDA (the Southernmost Disputed Area) (together, the “Disputed Areas”).

[9] Parties disagree as to whether the registered boundaries of Croft 1 accurately reflect the current legal boundaries of Croft 1, including historic enlargements.

The applicant’s case in summary

[10] The applicant seeks removal of the NDA and the SDA from the registered extent of Croft 1 on the basis that the true extent of Croft 1 comprises only the following three areas:

The subjects shown on the Land Court order and plan dated 26 September 1922 (production number 1), which shows Croft 1 (then referred to as “1 Bowglass”) as a single yellow‑outlined enclosure extending to approximately 8 acres (the “Original Subjects”);

Figure 3 - Detail of plan referred to in Land Court order dated 26 September 1922

The 1965 enlargement (the “Reseedings”). (The applicant relies on correspondence dated between April and October 1965 between Douglas Kesting and the crofters commission, which records the landlord’s agreement to let to the then crofter “an area of ground adjoining the main public road extending to some 8.6 acres or thereby which has already been reseeded by Mr Morrison.” The applicant submits that this description corresponds precisely to the fenced enclosure shown on the 1973 Ordnance Survey map (production number 17), lying east of the pre‑2004 public road.); and

The 1995 Apportionment (Area 3 on Figure 1 above) which allocates 23.900 hectares of common grazing to Croft 1 (the “1995 Apportionment”); less the following two areas:

Kosiden, which was the subject of a 1963 resumption (see applicant's production number 4); and

the subjects decrofted in 1999 (the original croft house site) (see applicant's production number 6).

[11] The Court should accordingly modify the registration so that it reflects the Original Subjects, under exception of the 1963 resumption and the 1999 decrofting, together with the 1995 Apportionment, and the Reseedings. The Disputed Areas, which are associated with the former public road and its verges, are not part of Croft 1. There was no lawful enlargement of Croft 1 associated with the old roadway and the construction of a new roadway.

The respondent’s position in outline

[12] Kosiden and the original croft house site do not form part of Croft 1. Kosiden was erroneously wrongly included in the registered extent of Croft 1 at first registration and should be removed. Quoad ultra the registered boundaries are correct. Croft 1 comprises the Original Subjects, the Reseedings, the 1995 Apportionment plus the Disputed Areas which are the subjects of a further enlargement associated with the old roadway following the re‑routing of the Stornoway to Tarbert road during the period 2004 to 2007. Esto evidence of any element is deficient, the Court should declare the registered boundary to be the appropriate boundary in terms of section 14(6) having regard to long‑standing physical demarcation, occupation and subsequent administrative acts.

Statutory framework

[13] Section 14 of Crofting Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 empowers the Court, on an application challenging first registration, to make an order that the entry be removed or modified, or to make no order. Where an application raises a question as to the boundaries of a croft but the evidence is insufficient to enable any boundary to be clearly determined, section 14(5) and (6) require the Court, if making an order to modify, to declare the boundary to be that which, in all the circumstances, it considers appropriate.

[14] The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993 governs how crofts are constituted and how they may be enlarged. Prior to 25 June 2007, section 4 provided that where the owner of land which was not itself a croft, and did not form part of a croft, agreed to let that land to a crofter, the land became part of the crofter’s existing croft on the date of entry if the parties agreed to that. However, if the combined area of the croft and the additional land was more than 30 hectares, and the combined rent was more than £100, the inclusion also required a direction from the Crofters Commission. The Commission could give such a direction only if the addition would benefit the croft and would not result in a croft substantially larger than 30 hectares or capable of being let at a rent substantially higher than £100 per year. After 25 June 2007, the rent threshold was removed, so that only the 30 hectare area threshold remained relevant to whether the Commission required to be involved.

Documents and plans

[15] The principal documents relevant to the boundaries and their evolution are:

The Land Court order of 26 September 1922 (County of Inverness RN3637) with plan, constituting the new holdings numbered 1 and 2.

The Land Court order of 27 May 1963 (County of Inverness RN10950) authorising resumption of 0.117 acres for the house site now known as Kosiden, with plan.

The decrofting direction dated 7 October 1999 in respect of the original croft house and garden.

The apportionment order of 15 June 1995 in favour of Croft 1.

Correspondence in 1965 between the landlord’s solicitor and the Crofters Commission relating to enlargement by addition of the reseeded land adjoining the then public road, giving an extent of about 8.6 acres and recording entry as at Martinmas 1965 and an increase in rent.

Ordnance Survey mapping from the early 1970s showing the route of the then public road and fenced enclosures.

The materials submitted at first registration in 2014, including the form A and plan prepared for the landlord.

Commission and landlord correspondence in 2013 to 2015 relating to the nomination and letting of Croft 1 to the respondent.

Witness evidence

[16] The Court heard evidence from the applicant and Mrs Macleod for the applicant; and from the respondent, Mr McSween, Ms Campbell, Mr Macleod, Mr Smith, Mr Maciver and Mrs Morrison for the respondent. All witnesses that gave evidence adopted the terms of their witness statements. No issues of credibility arise: we accept that all were seeking to give truthful evidence from their respective perspectives. Much of the evidence led was not ultimately significant to the question around which this dispute centres, that is to say, whether Croft 1 was enlarged during the period 2004-2007.

Evidence led for the applicant

[17] The applicant gave evidence and adduced evidence from Morag Macleod.

The applicant’s evidence

[18] The applicant inherited the tenancy of Croft 2 in 1999. A boundary dispute arose in 2023 when he proposed to replace perimeter fencing along the upper boundary of his croft adjacent to the disused former public road, which was superseded by a new road constructed around 2004. He believed neighbouring crofters had extended fencing into the disused road area and considered that he should be able to do likewise.

[19] In April and May 2023 he discussed boundaries with the respondent, who maintained that the two Disputed Areas formed part of Croft 1. He asked for supporting paperwork or maps but none were produced. At a site meeting the respondent showed a map which did not depict the Disputed Areas as part of Croft 1 and described the ground as “no man’s land”. He later discovered that Croft 1 had been registered in 2014, at a time when he had sublet Croft 2 to the respondent. He emphasised that he had received no notification of the application for registration or of the registration itself.

[20] The applicant spoke to a number of matters predating 2003 arising from his historical researches. Those events are not material to the question requiring determination, which is whether a landlord and crofter agreement occurred during the 2004 to 2007 road works. The boundaries of Croft 1 prior to that period are not in dispute

[21] The applicant obtained historic Ordnance Survey mapping and the Crofting Register extract and arranged for projection of the registered boundaries onto the 1973 map. He considered that this showed that Kosiden and the two Disputed Areas were wrongly included within the registered extent of Croft 1 and that the 1995 Apportionment was correctly plotted. He has identified no documentation in Crofting Commission files, correspondence or the Register of Crofts indicating any enlargement after 1995.

[22] During cross examination he accepted that he had never used, needed access to, or possessed the Disputed Areas. He regarded them as “no man’s land” that it “would be nice to have”. His interest is limited to the blue shaded area immediately above his croft. His application had initially challenged the inclusion of a larger area. He is unsure why he has restricted his position. He accepts that the 2014 registration materials show that the landlord proceeded on the basis of the boundaries as registered and that the Trust had not been asked to rectify or modify the entry.

[23] He observed what he believed to be boundary extensions or new fences erected by crofters at Bowglass up to the new road but did not discuss this with the respondent. He accepted there was a fence around the Reseedings and that he had had no discussions about it. The registered extent of Croft 1 does not affect his ability to move livestock, as he uses a trailer and his vehicular access is unaffected. He had been in communication with the Crofting Commission before applying to the Court but could not recall the details. His understanding of the boundaries developed over the course of the application as historical material came to light. He told North Harris Trust he would like the piece of land at the top of his croft and was told the matter was one for the Land Court.

Mrs Macleod’s evidence

[24] Mrs Macleod has lived in Ardvourlie all her life and now resides at Glenisle, a feu taken from Croft 2. She grew up in the croft house on Croft 2 and walked daily along what was then a single track public road. On the seaward side of that road there was a roadside fence which, in her recollection, ran from the corner of Mulag House towards a point just short of the culvert over the burn through Croft 2 and then tied into Croft 2 on the far side of the burn. That fence remained in the same position throughout her lifetime until the construction of the new road after the millennium. She spoke to various matters of local history, which are not material to the question requiring determination.

[25] Reseeding work on Croft 2 involved the spreading of sand (used as a conditioner and liming agent) on an old disused track near the croft entrance. This was carried out by family members with assistance from Donald John Morrison, the then crofter of Croft 1. The adjoining enclosure known locally as the Reseedings did not extend beyond the roadside fence and did not cross the burn or its culvert. Sand for that reseeding was deposited just inside a gate on the public roadside. Locally the Reseedings were not regarded as part of Croft 1.

[26] Peat cutting took place on land across the old public road and peats were stacked there before being transported home by hand. Movement between the croft house and the public road was not impeded because the roadside fence terminated at the far side of the burn. During the new road works, contractors removed the old fence and erected a new fence adjacent to the new road. In oral evidence she recalled that, when she was at school, the original fence lay on the south side of the watercourse and that the replacement fence did not follow the same line. She had no knowledge as to whether the Disputed Area had been added to Croft 1.

[27] The respondent gave evidence and adduced evidence from Ian McSween, Miranda Campbell, Alistair Macleod, Mark Smith, Alasdair Morrison, Michael Hunter, Colin Maciver and Catherine Morrison.

The respondent’s evidence

[28] The respondent was born in 1972. He is the tenant of Croft 1, having succeeded his uncle, Murdo Morrison, following Murdo’s death in 2010. His entry as tenant was recorded in the Register of Crofts in January 2015. Croft 1 comprises the Original Subjects, the roadside enclosure added in 1965 known as the Reseedings, the 1995 Apportionment and the Disputed Areas lying adjacent to the former public road.

[29] The Reseedings have formed part of Croft 1 since 1965, and their boundaries are reflected in long‑standing fences which, to the respondent’s knowledge, have not changed since at least the 1970s. During the period when Croft 2 was sublet to the respondent, neither he nor Murdo Morrison treated any part of the Reseedings as belonging to Croft 2.

[30] The Disputed Areas became part of Croft 1 when the public road was rerouted between about 2005 and 2007. Fences erected during the works enclosed those areas and remain in that position. The realignment works proceeded with the knowledge of Murdo Morrison and the landlord, and the enclosed areas have been possessed and worked with Croft 1 since at least 2007. Removal of the Disputed Areas would impede access to the Reseedings.

[31] The landlord submitted the 2014 application for first registration and relied on a plan prepared by SAC which followed the fences then present on the ground. The landlord accepted that fence based plan and used it for registration. The respondent understood the landlord and his predecessor as crofter to have proceeded on the shared basis that the fence lines represented the true extent of the croft. The inclusion of Kosiden was an unnoticed error.

[32] Public notice of registration was given by newspaper advertisement and a site notice. The applicant would, in any event, have been aware long before 2023 of the boundaries as physically occupied and of the extent later reflected in the Register.

[33] A decrofting direction in 2023 in respect of part of the former roadway area enabled the erection of the respondent’s house. The site was purchased from the landlord, and a dwellinghouse has now been constructed on the footing that the land formed part of Croft 1. The landlord continues to proceed on that basis. Were any part of the disputed ground held not to form part of Croft 1, the respondent would seek enlargement with the landlord’s support.

[34] Passages of the respondent’s evidence concerned fencing carried out in the 1990s by his uncle, family discussions about boundaries, and the limitations of historic plans. Those matters are peripheral and not relevant to the issue requiring determination.

[35] The respondent’s understanding of the current extent of Croft 1 derives from discussions within the family, including conversations with Murdo and Finlay Morrison, and from the fact that the fence lines present at the time of succession had long been treated by his predecessors as the operational boundaries. Maps were accepted as potentially imperfect, but the fences on the ground were regarded as determinative in practice. No fence lines have been moved during his tenure.

Ian McSween’s evidence

[36] Mr Ian McSween, born in 1949, is a lifelong resident of Scaladale and a crofter. He is familiar with both the old public road and the new one and has known successive crofters of Croft 1, including Murdo Morrison, Donald John Morrison and earlier members of the family.

[37] The respondent told him that he regarded the areas of the former roadway as having become part of Croft 1 following the rerouting of the public road. Mr McSween himself used the surface of the old roadway for loading sheep for transport because its condition made access straightforward.

[38] He recalled reseeding work at Scaladale in the early 1960s and understood that reseeding at Ardvourlie occurred around the same period. In his understanding, crofters affected by the realignment had taken in the additional areas lying between the old and new road fences, including parts of the former roadway. Murdo Morrison told him that Croft 1 had been enlarged as a consequence of the realignment.

[39] The applicant visited him in either 2023 or 2024, prior to the commencement of these proceedings, to ask about the boundary between the crofts. Mr McSween advised the applicant not to fall out with the respondent over the matter. He knows the applicant and the applicant’s family but has had no further involvement. He rejected any suggestion of “land grabbing”, describing such suggestions as “absolute rubbish”.

Miranda Campbell’s evidence

[40] Ms Campbell resides at Kosiden, now known as Seaforth, purchased with her late husband in 2000. She is the tenant crofter of croft 1 Bowglass, a tenancy previously held by her husband until his death in 2022.

[41] Between about 2003 and 2006 the widening and rerouting of the A859 caused significant disruption to croft 1 Bowglass, croft 1 North Bowglass and Croft 1 Ardvourlie. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar took land out of the Bowglass Common Grazings for the new road and embankments and, as a planning condition, fenced the common grazings from the new road. Rock spoil was deposited on croft 1 Bowglass and later covered with topsoil which subsequently washed off, altering drainage and leaving the lower part of the croft boggy. Rock spoil was also deposited on Croft 1 Ardvourlie in the area now occupied by the Norpower compound.

[42] A strip of land about the width of the old single track road was added to croft 1 Bowglass as compensation for disturbance.

[43] Her late husband dealt with all discussions with the Comhairle and she was not involved in detail. Her understanding is that an area of the old roadway was added to the Croft 1, although she does not know the detail of any discussions or agreements. Her only interest in the registered extent of Croft 1 Ardvourlie is that Kosiden, her house site, be removed from the registration. The respondent has not been a source of difficulty to her and she regards him and his wife as good neighbours. After this application commenced, the respondent informed her that her house had been included in the registered extent of his croft and undertook to have that error corrected.

Alistair Macleod’s evidence

[44] Mr Macleod was manager of North Harris Trust from 2013, having previously served as development officer from 2002. The respondent was ultimately nominated as tenant of Croft 1 after a period of vacancy following Murdo Morrison’s death.

[45] Mr Macleod submitted the registration application for Croft 1 in September 2014 on behalf of the landlord. The plan used for that application was prepared to follow the fences then present on the ground. In completing the application, he relied on information provided by the respondent as to boundaries. He did not investigate the historic evolution of the boundary, he did not scrutinise adjacent croft boundaries, and his working assumption was that crofters knew their own boundaries.

[46] The plan accompanying the application included areas of old roadway surface. Mr Macleod does not recall any discussion with the respondent about that particular feature, his understanding being that such operational matters would have been addressed during the road works between crofters and the Comhairle. He did not turn his mind to whether the inclusion of those areas reflected a prior legal enlargement.

[47] Kosiden should not have been included in the registration, it having been resumed in 1963. Mr Macleod did not know that at the time of submitting the application.

Mark Smith’s evidence

[48] Mr Mark Smith gave evidence by telephone from Madeira. He was formerly a resident engineer in the technical services department of Comhairle nan Eilean Siar and was involved throughout the project to reroute and upgrade the A859 between 2004 and 2007.

[49] When the new road was constructed, the Comhairle agreed to position the new fence line between the new road and the surface of the old single track roadway. Land that was not required for the scheme would ordinarily be returned, as the old roadway surface was of no use to the Comhairle. The fence line represented the minimum land take and was pegged out and agreed with crofters before erection. At Croft 1 Ardvourlie the old road surface was left unbroken at the request of Murdo Morrison, who had previously had a garage on the route of the then proposed new road which required to be demolished.

[50] Mr Smith had been shown a memorandum dated 9 May 2007, with an attached letter from the trust’s solicitor dated 8 May 2007, referring to the erection of the fence, together with a further memorandum concerning a meeting dated 25 June 2007. He accepted that although the memo was not issued on the same date as the meeting, it was possible that the meeting took place on 25 June and that the memo followed the usual practice of being sent out immediately.

[51] Land take plans were settled in advance with landlords and crofters, and amendments were made as required when the works were completed. Old road surfaces were normally broken up, reinstated with peat and returned to crofts or the estate once the Comhairle ceased occupation. Vacating the areas occupied depended on completion of reinstatement. Mr Smith did not know when, if at all, the old road was formally adopted.

[52] Mr Smith is not a specialist in crofting law. Croft boundaries were, in his understanding, a matter for the Trust as landlord. The fence erected by the Comhairle served to indicate the minimum land required for the works. The final fence line was pegged out and agreed with crofters and could, depending on stage, reflect the outcome of a resumption process. In relation to landscaping, the usual reinstatement was to break up the old surface and cover it with peat, but at Croft 1 Ardvourlie the old surface was left at Murdo Morrison’s request. Any departure from the standard reinstatement practice would have been agreed with Scottish Natural Heritage.

Alasdair Morrison’s evidence

[53] Alasdair Morrison is the tenant crofter of - and resides at - Croft 2, Bowglass, which was previously his grandparents’ croft. He has lived there since the age of 12, apart from a short period living away.

[54] He recalls the rerouting of the A859 in around 2004 to 2007 but does not remember exact dates. At Bowglass the new road was built through the common grazings. The Comhairle deposited gravel onto his croft and used it to cover the old road surface, then covered the gravel to some degree with soil. The Comhairle’s fencers removed the old fence and moved it up to the new road. If the fence had not been moved there would have been a large unused space between the fence and the road. Something similar happened at Croft 1 Bowglass and Croft 1 Ardvourlie, which were similarly affected by the road works. Murdo Morrison was the crofter at Croft 1 Ardvourlie at the time. Murdo asked the Comhairle to deposit spoil where the Norpower installation now stands. Beyond that, he has no specific knowledge of the croft boundary at Croft 1 Ardvourlie.

[55] He regards the present dispute as “ridiculous” and disputes over small pieces of ground as “pointless”.

Michael Hunter’s evidence

[56] Mr Hunter was born in 1988 and became manager of North Harris Trust in March 2020. Croft 1 Ardvourlie was registered before his time as manager. He met with the crofters in 2023 prior to commencement of the present application, but that meeting did not resolve matters.

[57] He signed a letter on behalf of North Harris Trust to Finlay Morrison dated 14 August 2025 (respondent’s production 59), it having been tabled and agreed at the North Harris Trust board meeting on 11 August 2025. In it the Trust undertakes to the respondent that if for any reason the Court determines that the extent of Croft 1 has been incorrectly registered, the Trust will enlarge and re‑let the croft to the respondent, the extent of the croft to be the extent of Croft 1 as currently registered (with the exception of Kosiden).

Colin Maciver’s evidence

[58] Mr Maciver is a civil engineering manager with Comhairle nan Eilean Siar. The Comhairle’s involvement in the Aline to Ardvourlie road improvement was limited to defining the boundary of the newly constructed road. Initial land plans were prepared during the design stage to enable discussions with landowners and grazing committees. Following completion, as built fence lines were surveyed to update the plans, which revealed that sections of the old single track road lay outside the land conveyed to the Comhairle. Meetings were held with estate representatives and grazing clerks to address treatment of resumed land. Simon Fraser of Anderson Macarthur, acting for North Harris Trust, advised that a legal process existed to return resumed land to crofting tenure. It was understood that old road sections would be added to adjacent crofts, with responsibility for amending and registering croft boundaries resting with the Trust, Anderson Macarthur, the grazings committee, and croft tenants.

Catherine Morrison’s evidence

[59] Catherine Morrison resides at 1A Ardvourlie with her husband, the respondent. Existing fences on Croft 1 have remained unchanged since her husband became tenant, and are in the same position as when Murdo Morrison held the tenancy. Murdo Morrison intended to leave the croft to the respondent. Following Murdo’s death, the North Harris Trust nominated the respondent as tenant. She recalls that prior to this, the respondent sub‑let Mr MacDonald’s croft at 2 Ardvourlie to assist him when the Crofting Commission raised absenteeism concerns. The respondent acted in good faith and the fences have not moved during the period of his tenancy.

Submissions for the applicant

[60] Mr Kermack adopted his written submissions which are available in the Court process.

[61] In a section 14 application, the Court requires to determine whether the boundaries shown in the Crofting Register accurately reflect the legal boundaries of the unregistered croft, rather than boundaries of current occupation. Where the evidence allows a boundary to be clearly determined, the Court must recognise and give effect to that boundary; it has no discretion to substitute what it considers “appropriate”: Macaulay v Morrison, Scottish Land Court, unreported, 13 March 2017 at [28] and [29]. Only where section 14(6) applies, and the evidence is insufficient to allow any boundary to be identified, may the Court declare a boundary that it considers appropriate in the circumstances.

[62] In the instant case the Court should make an order under section 14(4)(b) of the 2010 Act modifying the Crofting Register entry for Croft 1 by removing the Disputed Areas so as to align the registration with the legal boundaries of Croft 1, under reference to:

the boundaries shown on the plan annexed to the Land Court order of 26 September 1922, subject to the area resumed by order of 27 May 1963 and the land decrofted by direction dated 7 October 1999;

the land apportioned by the apportionment order dated 15 June 1995; and

the fenced enclosure east of the former public road shown on the 1973 Ordnance Survey.

[63] The registered boundaries of the NDA do not reflect the legal boundaries of the unregistered croft. The correct extent of that northern section of Croft 1 is shown on the plan annexed to the Land Court order of 26 September 1922, which depicts a single enclosed holding of about 8 acres bisected by a track. The 1922 plan represents the original definitive boundary of the NDA.

[64] Correspondence dated 24 April 1957 from Stewart, Rule & Co., solicitors, to the Crofters Commission confirms that the rights of the tenants of 1 and 2 Bowglass were constituted by the final order of 26 September 1922 and that there had been no change to the extent of either croft between 1922 and 1957. That demonstrates that the registered extent of the NDA does not reflect the legal boundaries of Croft 1.

[65] The original croft house was decrofted by the direction dated 7 October 1999. The stated area of 0.304 hectares is plainly a decimal error; boundary measurements indicate an area of about 0.0304 hectares. The house site removed from crofting by this direction is wrongly included within the registered boundary of the NDA.

[66] The 1963 resumption of the Kosiden house site removed land from the NDA and did not add to it, yet the registration wrongly incorporates the entire Kosiden plot back into Croft 1.

[67] To the extent that the registered extent of the NDA includes land which was never part of Croft 1, its inclusion in the registration is an obvious error.

[68] The SDA adjoins an enlargement of Croft 1 made in 1965 of approximately 8.6 acres adjoining the then public road. The enlargement is evidenced by contemporaneous correspondence and corroborated by witness testimony regarding reseeding within a fenced enclosure.

[69] On 29 April 1965, Douglas Kesting, solicitor, wrote seeking procedural guidance on adding approximately 8 to 9 acres to Croft 1. On 28 May 1965 the Crofters Commission advised that an enlargement required intimation under section 2(2) of the 1961 Act, confirming the landlord’s agreement to let the land in enlargement of the holding. On 31 May 1965 Mr Kesting stated he would complete missives once a definitive plan was obtained and would then notify the Commission. The letter of 15 October 1965 records that an area of ground adjoining the then main public road, extending to about 8.6 acres, had been added to Croft 1 with entry at Martinmas 1965 and that the ground had already been reseeded by the crofter.

[70] Mrs Macleod’s evidence identifies the reseeding area as the fenced roadside enclosure long known locally as “the reseedings” and confirms that this was the only ground reseeded by Mr Morrison. Read as a whole, the sequence of correspondence establishes a single enlargement at the reseeding area now identified as Area 2, and this is corroborated by witness testimony.

[71] Area 3 corresponds to the 1995 Apportionment to Croft 1. Its boundaries are not disputed and the applicant seeks no order in respect of this area.

[72] There is no evidence of any enlargement of Croft 1 following construction of the new road from 2004. By 1995, the area of Croft 1 already exceeded 30 hectares (comprising the 8 acre original holding and the 8.6 acre 1965 enlargement together with the 23.9 hectare apportionment made in 1995, producing a total of approximately 30.62 hectares). Any subsequent enlargement could only take place under section 4(1)(b) of the 1993 Act, which required a joint application by landlord and crofter to the Crofting Commission and a direction from the Commission before the land could form part of the croft. No such application or direction exists and so no enlargement could have occurred during the period of the road realignment.

[73] The statutory framework required notice to the Crofting Commission of any such enlargement, or a joint application for enlargement. No such notice or record exists. The respondent’s case that there was an agreement with the landlord is unsupported and indicates, at best, tolerance rather than an implied agreement. Fencing erected during roadworks does not establish an enlargement under section 4 of the 1993 Act.

[74] In supplementary written submissions the applicant founded on section 1(9) of the Roads (Scotland) Act 1984 and on London Borough of Southwark v Transport for London [2018] UKSC 63, submitting that the former public road and its verges remained vested in the roads authority within the zone of ordinary use, and were inalienable for so long as that responsibility persisted; and accordingly, as at June 2007, the landlord had no power to agree an enlargement of Croft 1 into any part of the former roadway area.

Submissions for the respondent

[75] Mr Rudd adopted his written submissions which are available in the Court process.

[76] The onus lies on the applicant to prove that, on the balance of probabilities, the areas he seeks to remove should not form part of Croft 1. The task of the Court is to identify the status quo ante and follow it where the evidence is sufficient. Only where the evidence is insufficient does section 14(6) empower the Court to determine and impose what it considers to be an “appropriate” boundary.

[77] The only parts of the registered extent of Croft 1 now in dispute are those shaded blue on the applicant’s production 20, other than Kosiden, which parties are agreed should be removed. Quoad ultra the boundaries should remain as registered.

[78] The applicant lacks a practical interest to object to the registered boundaries of Croft 1, given that that he does not aver that the areas he seeks to have removed from Croft 1 form part of Croft 2 or of the common grazings.

[79] There is supporting evidence from multiple independent sources consistent with the respondent’s understanding of the boundary. The original holding was created in 1922. Its extent is shown in the plan appended to the Land Court order and the Board of Agriculture application.

[80] The 1995 Apportionment is uncontroversial and is properly included in Croft 1.

[81] The Reseeding Area was added to the croft in 1965. The only difference between parties in respect of this area relates to the northern extent of the reseeding area. The fenced and occupied extent of this area extends further north into part of the applicant’s blue-shaded area, and has done so since at least the 1970s and certainly since the 1990s. Esto any part of this ground does not form part of the 1965 enlargement, it was added during the later boundary adjustments associated with construction of the new road. IACS maps produced by the respondent show the areas the crofter claimed and worked, albeit these indicate usage rather than legal boundaries. With reference to the enlargement of Croft 1 during the period 2004 ‑ 2007 at the old roadway area, enlargement of a croft could occur by agreement between a landlord and a crofter in terms of section 4 of the 1993 Act as it then stood, without formal requirements for written form. The statutory notification requirement was administrative rather than constitutive. On the evidence, an agreement between landlord and crofter existed by 25 June 2007, and the croft as enlarged (excluding the common grazing) remained under 30 hectares and the rent remained under £100 per annum. The 30 hectare threshold in section 4(1)(b) of the 1993 Act as it then stood is not here engaged. The “area of the croft” for the purposes of that provision excludes any common grazing. The 23.9 hectare apportionment made in 1995 remains part of the common grazings and does not alter the extent of the in‑bye land.

[82] The fencing erected during the road re‑routing was done on the basis that the fenced area was being added to crofts in Ardvourlie and Bowglass. The evidence from their officers demonstrates that the Comhairle’s understanding was that the fenced land was being incorporated into the crofts and that the landlord’s factor participated in those discussions. Similar enlargements occurred at Bowglass. The applicant raised no issue with the fence lines before 2023 despite having been the crofter of Croft 2 since 1999.

[83] A number of outward actions evidence the existence of such an agreement, including: instructions given for fencing; what the respondent was told by Murdo Morrison; the absence of any separate occupancy arrangement; the landlord’s actions in relation to the 2014 letting, the first registration, the decrofting and disposition for the respondent’s house site, and later dealings with Norpower; and confirmation from the landlord that they understood the registered extent to be the correct extent. If, however, the Court finds that the evidence does not allow the boundaries of the alleged enlargement to be clearly determined, the Court should exercise its power under section 14(6) to declare the boundary which it considers most appropriate in all the circumstances. The current registered boundary represents the appropriate and pragmatic boundary, reflecting long‑standing de facto possession, decisions taken in reliance upon it, the concurrence of landlord and tenant and the absence of any practical benefit to the applicant from alteration.

[84] In supplementary written submissions, the respondent submitted that the Roads (Scotland) Act 1984 regulates the public management of roads and does not, by virtue of section 1(9), confer any heritable right of ownership on the roads authority. Once the new A859 was brought into use and the associated fencing was erected in 2004 and 2005, the former public road ceased to be used for its previous purpose. There is no competing title to the areas now in dispute, the North Harris Trust having acquired Title number INV29919 in 2003.

Decision and reasons

[85] In the particular circumstances of this case, determination of the precise legal boundaries of Croft 1 is, to a degree, a sterile exercise in respect that the landlord has undertaken to the respondent that, if for any reason the Court were to determine that the extent of Croft 1 had been incorrectly registered, the landlord will enlarge and re‑let the croft to the respondent at the currently registered extent (under exception of Kosiden). The practical outcome for the parties will be materially the same whether the matter is determined on the primary basis of enlargement or, failing that, on the respondent’s alternative case under section 14(6). The Court must nonetheless determine whether, as at the date of first registration in 2014, the legal boundary of Croft 1 includes the Disputed Areas.

[86] We find, on the evidence, that it does. We do so, not because of any constitutive effect of the fencing erected during the road realignment works (there is none), but rather on account of the crofter’s and landlord’s subsequent and consistent treatment of that fence line as the de facto boundary of the croft. In the context of section 4 of the 1993 Act as it then stood, enlargement did not require written form, nor any particular formality, provided that landlord and crofter reached consensus as to the subjects to be added. Such consensus may be inferred from their conduct. The sequence of outward acts (the pegging out of the fence line in consultation with the then crofter, the landlord’s engagement in the treatment of reinstated ground, the subsequent reliance on the same boundary at first registration in 2014 and the landlord’s use of that boundary in later decroftings) is consistent with a shared intention that the subjects enclosed by the fence formed part of the croft tenancy, and is inconsistent with mere tolerance or convenience.

[87] Events prior to the 21st century were ultimately uncontroversial. Croft 1 was constituted in 1922 in the terms of the Land Court’s order and plan. In 1963 Kosiden was resumed. Parties agree that Kosiden ought not to have been included at first registration and must now be removed. In 1965 there was an enlargement in favour of Croft 1 to the fenced roadside enclosure locally known as the Reseedings. In 1995 an apportionment of Area 3 was made in favour of Croft 1. The dispute between parties turns on whether there was a lawful enlargement associated with the road realignment. The Disputed Areas lie adjacent to the new A859 as defined on the ground by the fence erected during the 2004 to 2007 road works.

[88] On the evidence, and in particular the account given by Mr Smith of the pegging out and erection of the fence line during the road realignment project, we are satisfied that by the conclusion of the works in 2007 the physical boundary adjoining Croft 1 had been delineated in a manner known to, and not objected to by, the then crofter and the landlord.

[89] In assessing the competing accounts of the 2004 to 2007 period we place particular weight on the respondent’s evidence. He was a careful witness and we found him credible and reliable on the central matters. His evidence was consistent with that of the witnesses from the Trust and the Comhairle, which we also accept. We accept also the limited but consistent evidence of Mrs Morrison. By contrast, the applicant was not in a position to speak to Murdo Morrison’s dealings with the Comhairle or the landlord, and his understanding of the boundary does not derive from direct knowledge of those dealings. The available evidence, including circumstantial evidence, favours the respondent. The applicant’s lack of use of the Disputed Areas is not determinative of their legal status, but it is a further relevant adminicle when assessing the competing reconstructions of the post 2004 position, although not, for the avoidance of doubt, indicative of any diminution of rights through disuse.

[90] Section 4 of the 1993 Act, as it stood at the material time, permitted enlargement by agreement between owner and crofter, with effect from the agreed date of entry. No particular formality was prescribed where the 30 hectare threshold in section 4(1)(b) was not crossed, although notice to the Commission under section 4(4) was required thereafter. We infer from the available evidence the existence of an agreement between the landlord and the then crofter, Murdo Morrison, that the Disputed Areas would form part of Croft 1. The Trust and Murdo Morrison were evidently both content to proceed on that basis without demur. The sequence of outward acts is indicative of agreement: fence lines erected and thereafter adopted as the operational boundary; the landlord’s involvement in the 2007 discussions; the use of a fence based plan for first registration by the landlord in 2014; the nomination and letting at that extent; and subsequent transactions, including decrofting for the respondent’s house site and later dealings in which the landlord proceeded on the footing that the Disputed Areas formed part of Croft 1. The Trust’s later letter of August 2025 further vouches that understanding, (other than as regards Kosiden). We therefore hold that by 2007 at the latest the landlord and the then crofter had agreed that the Disputed Areas would form part of Croft 1 and that the enlargement took effect from that time. This consensus between landlord and crofter was reached during the period of the realignment works and, in any event, by their conclusion in 2007, at a time when the pre‑existing form of section 4 of the 1993 Act remained in force. For the purposes of section 4(1)(a), the effective date of entry for the added strip is the conclusion of the works in 2007. The subjects of enlargement are identified by reference to the as built fence and the adjacent former roadway, which landlord and crofter thereafter adopted in all dealings.

[91] In identifying the subjects by reference to the as built fence and the adjacent former roadway, we are not creating a new boundary but locating, on the balance of probabilities, the boundary adopted by landlord and crofter at the material time. The statutory requirement is one of consensus, not paperwork. Section 4(4) notice to the Commission is not constitutive: enlargement takes effect from the date of entry agreed between landlord and crofter. While the absence of contemporaneous notification or rent adjustment is a relevant consideration, it is not determinative. In this case, the landlord’s consistent treatment of the disputed subjects in the years following the works — including the first registration and subsequent decroftings — provides persuasive evidence that any omission to intimate was administrative rather than substantive. The Court therefore proceeds on the basis that the enlargement was effected through agreement and actings, rather than through formal documentation.

[92] The applicant founds on the absence of a Commission notice and on the lack of express missives or rent adjustment. Those are relevant considerations. Again, however, they are not determinative. Subsequent landlord conduct consistently proceeded on the basis that enlargement had occurred. In any event, the subsequent first registration in 2014, which proceeded upon the fence based plan adopted by the landlord, brought the extent to the attention of the Commission. On the whole evidence we do not regard the absence of earlier notification as displacing the inference of agreement. There was at no stage any separate licence or seasonal letting of the disputed strip, which is consistent with its being treated by landlord and crofter as part of the croft rather than as the subject of mere tolerance or permissive occupation.

[93] Section 4(1)(b) of the 1993 Act prior to 25 June 2007 requires the Court to assess the area of Croft 1 exclusive of any common pasture or grazing land held therewith. An apportionment is land within the common grazings allocated to a crofter’s exclusive use. It does not, however, alter the extent of the croft in-bye. It follows that the apportioned area is left out of account when applying the 30 hectare threshold. Whether a Commission direction under section 4(1)(b) was required turns on whether the area of the croft excluding any apportionment exceeds 30 hectares. It follows also that the applicant’s calculation of approximately 30.62 hectares, which treats the 23.9 hectare apportionment as being part of Croft 1, proceeds on a mistaken legal basis, and that the in‑bye area of Croft 1 remained well below the 30‑hectare threshold throughout.

[94] With reference to parties’ submissions anent the Roads (Scotland) Act 1984, vesting under section 1(9) is functional and expressly stated to confer no heritable title on the roads authority. The statutory vesting endures only for so long as land serves a road purpose. By the time the new A859 was brought into use, the former single track road at Ardvourlie had ceased to serve any road purpose. The Comhairle’s reinstatement decisions, including the agreement reached with Murdo Morrison as to the treatment of the old surface, are consistent with the authority no longer maintaining or requiring the land for road purposes. In those circumstances, nothing in the 1984 Act precluded the landlord and crofter from agreeing that the land contiguous to the croft would form part of Croft 1.

[95] Mr Kermack invited the Court to hold that no enlargement occurred and, esto the legal boundary could not be discerned, to determine an appropriate boundary under section 14(6). In our view, there is sufficient evidence for the boundaries - and the fact of enlargement - to be identified on the balance of probabilities. If, however, we are wrong about that and should instead have considered that the evidential picture at the locus of the former roadway to be insufficiently clear, we would, in that event, have declared, in terms of section 14(6), that the present registered fence line is, in all the circumstances, the most coherent, intelligible and administratively workable boundary. It has been visible and acted upon for almost two decades, has underpinned landlord and tenant decisions made in good faith, and has been reflected in subsequent transactions. We also take into account the landlord’s stated willingness to enlarge and re‑let Croft 1 so as to include the Disputed Areas if the registration were to be found inaccurate; and the absence of any better competing claim (or indeed, any claim at all) by the applicant to that ground.

[96] In the whole circumstances we shall modify the Crofting Register entry by removing Kosiden. Quoad ultra we shall refuse the application. All questions of expenses are reserved.
